opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a very simple bottleneck: data. If you look at why large language models took off, it's because the internet had already accumulated trillions of tokens of text. Nobody had to go out and collect it specifically for training. Robotics doesn't have that. There is no "internet of robot actions." Every trajectory showing how a robot arm grasps a cup, opens a drawer, or hands something to a person has to be produced somehow, and if you rely only on real-world teleoperation, it's extremely slow and expensive. You need the hardware, the operators, the scenes, the objects. Even a well-funded team can collect thousands or maybe tens of thousands of hours. That's tiny compared with what a generalist model needs.

So early on, our team made a bet that the bulk of the training data for embodied intelligence, especially for the foundational skills like grasping, placing, and navigation, should come from simulation and synthetic generation. In simulation, we can procedurally generate huge numbers of object assets, randomize lighting, materials, textures, camera positions, and physical parameters, and then use planning algorithms to automatically produce successful grasps and trajectories. That lets us scale to billions of frames at a cost that real-world collection simply can't match.

The second reason is diversity. Real data tends to be concentrated in a few labs or a few factory settings. When you deploy a robot into a new pharmacy, a new retail store, or someone's home, it meets objects and layouts it has never seen. Synthetic data lets us deliberately cover the long tail: transparent objects, reflective objects, cluttered shelves, odd shapes. That diversity is what gives the model real generalization rather than memorization.

Of course, people always ask about the sim-to-real gap. That's real, and a lot of our research effort has gone into closing it: better rendering, better physics, domain randomization, and designing the model's inputs and outputs so they transfer more robustly. Our view is not that real data is useless. Real data is very valuable for post-training and fine-tuning, for the last stretch of performance in a specific scenario. But the pyramid should be wide at the bottom with synthetic data and narrower at the top with real data.

When we show a robot picking up items it has never encountered, zero-shot, in a real store, that ability came largely from the synthetic pipeline. That's why I see it as central. Without it, every new deployment becomes a new data collection project, and you can't scale. With it, deployment becomes much closer to a software problem, and that's the only way embodied AI becomes a real industry.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data is central to scaling deployment and describes a zero-shot real-store example, but it does not connect the pipeline to achieving small-scale commercial robot deployment.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts synthetic and real data but gives no estimate that real-world data is about one percent or less of the team's training data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The short answer is that real-world robot data is the most expensive thing in this entire field, and synthetic data is the only lever we found that scales.

Think about what it takes to collect one teleoperation demonstration. You need a physical robot, a trained operator, a scene that someone set up by hand, and then you throw most of it away because the operator hesitated or the gripper slipped. If you want a grasping model that generalizes across thousands of object categories, you cannot get there by paying people to wiggle a controller. The internet gave language models trillions of tokens for free. Robotics has no equivalent, so we had to build one.

So from the beginning we decided to treat simulation as the primary data source rather than a supplement. Our pipeline takes large collections of object meshes, randomizes the physics, the lighting, the camera placement, the clutter, and then generates grasp labels or manipulation trajectories at a scale that is simply impossible physically. We are talking billions of grasp poses. Nobody is going to collect that in a lab.

The reason it works for deployment specifically is that the sim-to-real gap has gotten much narrower than people assume, especially for geometry-based tasks. When your policy consumes point clouds or depth rather than RGB, the domain gap is mostly about sensor noise and partial observation, and you can model those explicitly. We spent a lot of effort on rendering realistic depth artifacts. Once that is done, a model trained on synthetic data transfers to a new robot, a new camera, a new warehouse, with almost no fine-tuning. That is what customers actually care about. They do not want a demo that worked once in our lab.

There is also a feedback loop that matters. When a deployment fails on some weird transparent bottle or a flexible cable, we do not go collect ten thousand new real examples. We add that category to the generator, regenerate overnight, and retrain. Failures become a specification for the next batch of data. That turns a research problem into an engineering problem, and engineering problems are the ones you can actually ship on a schedule.

I would not say real data is useless. We use a small amount for validation and for calibrating the gap. But I think the teams that bet entirely on real-world collection are betting that the cost curve will come down fast enough, and I am not convinced it will. Simulation compute gets cheaper every year. Human operators do not.

r001.rationale: The response presents the team's synthetic-data pipeline as enabling deployment, but does not identify small-scale commercial robot deployment or clearly attribute that specific achievement to a self-developed pipeline.

r002.rationale: It describes real-world data as a small amount used for validation and calibration, but gives no one-percent-or-less figure for the team's training data.

astra-6.text:
I see it as central because deploying robots is fundamentally a generalization problem. A robot might succeed in a controlled setup, but in a new environment, the objects, lighting, clutter, and camera angles all change. Collecting real-world demonstrations for every combination is very difficult.

A synthetic-data pipeline gives us a way to systematically vary those conditions and generate training experience at scale. But the important part is the feedback loop: we test on real robots, identify where they fail, and use those failures to guide what we generate next. That makes the pipeline a way to turn deployment experience into better training data.

It doesn’t eliminate the need for real-world data or testing. It helps us use that expensive real-world experience more efficiently, so we can make progress beyond a single successful demo.

r001.rationale: The response calls the synthetic-data pipeline central to progress, but does not state that it enabled small-scale commercial robot deployment.

r002.rationale: It says real-world demonstrations are difficult to collect and that real-world data remains necessary, but gives no estimate of its share of training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as central because deploying robots is fundamentally a generalization problem. A robot can succeed in one setup, but we need it to keep working when the objects, lighting, backgrounds, or arrangements change. Collecting real-world demonstrations for every combination is very difficult.

A synthetic-data pipeline gives us a systematic way to generate that variation and target the cases where the robot struggles. We can use real-world failures to guide what we generate next, train on those examples, and then test again on the robot.

The key is that generating more data isn’t the goal by itself. The goal is to generate data that improves performance in the real world. That feedback loop is what makes the pipeline so valuable: each deployment helps us improve the training data for the next one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the synthetic-data pipeline helps improve real-world performance, but does not attribute the team’s small-scale commercial robot deployment to a self-developed pipeline.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no proportion for real-world data in the team’s training data.
